title: Do the two patterns hold for negatives and fractions?
description: The proofs in the book used letters and only the distributive property, so nothing in them is tied to counting numbers. The board then tests the first pattern with a negative number and a fraction, and the second with two negative numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: a proof written with letters holds for every number the letters can stand for. Watch for students who think that patterns found from counting-number examples stay inside the counting numbers.

source: Figure it Out (squares and patterns, question 4)
video_script.why: The child has seen both patterns work for counting numbers, but has not asked what the letter proof says about other kinds of numbers.
video_script.substitution: Read the letter proof for what it used, and test a negative number and a fraction, as the examples in the book tested counting numbers.
video_script.anchor: the two patterns from the book, each written with letters
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, both patterns hold for every number, including negatives and fractions.

final_answer.value: Yes; they hold for all numbers, including negative integers and fractions
final_answer.spoken: yes, both patterns hold for every number, including negatives and fractions

maths_rules: both proofs use only the distributive property, which holds for negative integers and fractions
video_script.design: One idea: the letter proof never used a counting number, so it holds for negatives and fractions, which two tests confirm. Both pattern cards stay on the stage.

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Your book wrote the first pattern with letters. Twice eigh squared plus b squared is eigh plus b squared plus eigh minus b squared.
<bookmark mark='two'/>The second pattern is eigh plus b times eigh minus b, which equals eigh squared minus b squared.

narration: <bookmark mark='proof'/>Step one, see what the proofs used. The book proved both patterns with letters, and only the distributive property.

narration: <bookmark mark='dist'/>Step two, the distributive property holds for negative integers, and for fractions too.
<bookmark mark='none'/>The proofs never used a counting number, so the patterns carry over to them.
<bookmark mark='pick'/>Step three, test the first pattern. Take eigh as minus three, and b as one half.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Twice the sum of squares, nine and one quarter, is eighteen and one half.
<bookmark mark='r1'/>Minus three plus one half is minus two and one half. Its square is six and one quarter.
<bookmark mark='r2'/>Minus three minus one half is minus three and one half. Its square is twelve and one quarter.
<bookmark mark='tick'/>Adding those two squares gives eighteen and one half. Both sides agree.
<bookmark mark='pick'/>Step four, put the second pattern back in the question. Take eigh as minus five, and b as two.
<bookmark mark='sums'/>Minus five plus two is minus three, and minus five minus two is minus seven.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Minus three times minus seven is twenty one.
<bookmark mark='right'/>On the other side, twenty five minus four is also twenty one.

beats.on_screen: Answer: yes, they hold for all numbers, including negative integers and fractions
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes, both patterns hold for every number, including negatives and fractions.
